metadata.title: Pimpinella anisum L. Essential Oil a Valuable Antibacterial and Antifungal Alternative

result.passage:
L80: In the case of the P. aeruginosa standard strain, the inhibition value revealed the anise essential oil’s great potency, confirming that the antimicrobial potential of anise essential oils varies between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, due probably to density variations in the bacterial cell wall. As we know, essential oils are in preponderance lipophilic, and this is why they are rapidly absorbed by Gram-positive bacteria due to their dense layer (especially of lipophilic phospholipids in their cell walls).
L81: This is why all studies tackling this issue could be considered of help. We consider that this class of studies is performed to develop the associative features of phyto-therapeutic means with other structures such as chemotherapeutics, sulfonamides, or antibiotics with the aim of gathering new efficient associated phyto-structures especially where the efficacy of anti-infectious classes is compromised by the resistance phenomena.
L82: 4. Materials and Methods
L83: The 100% pure anise Pimpinella anisum-Apiaceae (Umberlliferae) essential oil conditioning (Aromatics International) used in the study (Batch no. ANS-103/09.20.2020) was purchased from a local herbal store. According to the product’s information sheet, the manufacturer extracted the essential oil by steam distillation from organically grown brown pods of anise seed flowers, with a yield of 2–4%. Organoleptically, the oil has a grassy, sweet aroma with a slightly spicy (licorice-like) smell; its color is pale yellow with a medium viscosity.
L84: The chromatographic and microbiological analysis of anise essential oil was carried out within the Interdisciplinary Research Platform and the Toxicology—Pharmacology Research Laboratory within the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine Timișoara.
L85: 4.1. The GC/MS Compounds Analysis in P. anisum Essential Oil
L86: The analysis of the anise essential oil sample taken in the study was carried out using the Agilent Technology 7820A gas chromatograph, coupled with the Agilent MSD 5975 mass spectrometer (Agilent Scientific, Santa Clara, CA, USA) and with a DB WAX capillary column (30 m × 250 pm × 0.25 µm). Helium was used with a mass flow rate of 1 mL × min. For the separation of compounds, the following oven program was used: at 40 °C for 1 min, at 5 °C for 1 min, and raised to 210 °C for 5 min.
L87: The temperatures for the injector and ion source were 250 and 150 °C, respectively. The injection volume was 1 µL of each pure, solvent-free oil or mixture at a ratio of 1:20.
L88: The volatile compounds were identified using the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) spectrum library. This was conducted by comparing the mass spectra with the ones stored in the NIST 02, (Wiley 275 libraries). The percentage value of individual components was calculated based on GC peak areas without making use of any correction factors.
L89: 4.2. Determination of Antimicrobial Activity of P. anisum Essential Oils
L90: The antimicrobial activity was tested in triplicate. Bacterial strain suspensions in BHI were used as a positive Control. Over each bacterial suspension well, the essential oil of anise was used directly by adding in increasing amounts as 2, 4, 8, and 10 µL / well. Plates were covered and left overnight at 37 °C; then, the OD (optical density) was measured at 590 nm using a Bio-Rad PR 1100 Elisa reader (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc., Hercules, CA, USA).
L91: The average values of determinations were expressed statistically by one-way ANOVA. The differences were considered significant when p < 0.05 or lower.
L92: Broth Micro Dilution Method
L93: Among the most basic antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods is the broth microdilution method. This procedure tests 2-fold dilutions of the antimicrobial agent being assessed in 96-well micro titer plates filled with a liquid growth medium. Each plate is inoculated with microbes prepared in the same medium after dilution of the standardized microbial suspension adapted to the McFarland scale of 0.5.
L94: After inoculation, the 96-well microtiter plate is incubated under appropriate conditions according to the microorganism tested.
L95: The Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration of antimicrobial agent that completely inhibits the growth of the organism in the microdilution wells. The broth microdilution method has been standardized by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) for testing aerobic bacteria, yeasts, and filamentous fungi. The European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) broth microdilution method is similar to that of CLSI, with modifications typically relating to some of the test parameters, such as inoculum preparation, inoculum size, and MIC reading. The reference strains (ATCC) for the in vitro testing used were Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC 25923), Escherichia coli (ATCC 25922), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 27853), Streptococcus pyogenes (ATCC 19615), and Candida albicans (ATCC 10231), provided from the Microbiology Lab facility, within the ULS “King Mihai I” from Timisoara.
L96: All samples were run in triplicate. A fresh culture dilution of 10−3 with an inoculum equivalent to a 0.5 McFarland standard was prepared and used. The ATCC strains used were revitalized in Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth (Oxoid, CM1135) (Oxoid Ltd., Basingstoke, UK) overnight at 37 °C and then plated on BHI agar for 24 h at 37 °C. Dilution was performed to an optical density (OD) of 0.5 McFarland standard (1.5 × 108 CFU/mL) using BHI broth.
L97: The resulting suspensions were assayed using a 96-well flat-bottom microdilution plate with a usable volume of 200 µL. Using a Calibra 852 digital multi-channel pipette (Socorex Isba S.A. Ecublens, Switzerland), 100 µL of suspension was placed in each well.
L98: 4.3. Statistical Analysis
L99: The obtained results were presented as an arithmetic mean and SEM (Standard Error of the Mean) and were subjected to statistical analysis using one-way ANOVA (analysis of variance) with Bonferroni’s multiple comparison test. Statistically significant differences were considered when p < 0.05 or lower. The GraphPad Prism 6.0 software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, USA) was utilized for the analysis.
L100: 5. Conclusions
L101: A chromatographic analysis of anise essential oil confirmed the massive presence of polyphenolic compounds. The antimicrobial activity of Pimpinella anisum essential oil was mainly related to its phenolic content, with propenyl-anisum, limonene, and anisole being preponderant. To this aim, anise essential oil had certain antimicrobial activity against both the Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens tested. The highest percentages of inhibition were found in order on the Pseudomonas aeruginosa (109.84%) and Staphylococcus aureus (41.21%) strains but also with excellent antifungal activity against Candida albicans (72.04%).
L102: Figure 1: Streptococcus pyogenes—mean values of the three determinations for the Control and the four dilutions tested (where *** means p < 0.001).
L103: Figure 2: Pseudomonas aeruginosa—mean values of the three determinations for the Control and the four dilutions tested (where *** means p < 0.001).
L104: Figure 3: Staphylococcus aureus—mean values of the three determinations for the Control and the four tested dilutions (where *** means p < 0.001).
L105: Figure 4: Escherichia coli—mean values of the three determinations for the Control and the four tested dilutions (where *** means p < 0.001).
L106: Figure 5: Candida albicans—mean values of the three determinations for the Control and the four tested dilutions (where *** means p < 0.001 and * means p < 0.05).
L107: Table 1: Compounds identified in anise essential oil.
L108: Compound | R. Time | %

L110: 3-carene | 9.847 | 1.327

template.purpose: Find the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of a compound against a bacterial strain: 2-fold serial dilution in cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth, a standard inoculum added 1:1, overnight growth, turbidity read. A non-kinase negative control for routing.
notes: 463100 and 624097 are checkerboard synergy assays (compound x imipenem); only their shared broth-microdilution conditions (medium, inoculum, volume, incubation, readout) are used here.
Three of the four AIDs are from one Scripps project (metallo-beta-lactamase inhibitors). PubChem 'Activity outcome method' is 'Other' for 449774, 463100, 624097 and 'Confirmatory' for 1503.

The Opentrons exemplar is on the main branch, not this one: Opentrons/MIC_2Fold_Dilution_1Antibiotic_1Strain_200uL_modified.py. Its write-up (.docx) names both CAMHB and 'regular M9 broth' for the broth; the script's liquid label says CAMHB.
Inoculum: each source adds about 1e6 CFU/mL in an equal volume, so wells start near 5e5 CFU/mL (derived).

result.lab_yaml:
# What this lab can actually do: the instruments, the labware on hand, and the conditions available.
#
# This is a capability model, not an equipment list. `execution/feasibility.py` reads it to answer "can we run
# this experiment, and if not, why not" as arithmetic rather than judgement, and the agent can read it so that it
# proposes experiments this lab can run instead of ones it cannot.
#
# Most of it is taken from the team's real OT-2 protocol (Opentrons/MIC_2Fold_Dilution_1Antibiotic_1Strain_200uL
# _modified.py and its write-up), which is the only verified record of the deck we have. Anything not visible in
# that protocol is marked TODO(final) and should be confirmed by whoever is standing next to the robot.

instruments:
  - id: ot2
    kind: liquid_handler
    model: Opentrons OT-2
    api_level: "2.28"              # the level Emmy's protocol targets; the robot software must be at least this
    deck_slots: 11                 # 1-11 usable, 12 is the fixed trash
    pipettes:
      # from the protocol: load_instrument("p300_multi", "left")
      - mount: left
        model: p300_multi
        channels: 8                # one command moves a whole column
        min_uL: 20
        max_uL: 300
      # the write-up says the P20 "is not used and can stay mounted on the right"
      # TODO(final): confirm it is mounted, and whether it is a gen2 and single or multi
      - mount: right
        model: p20_single_gen2
        channels: 1
        min_uL: 1
        max_uL: 20
        mounted: unconfirmed

  - id: cytation
    kind: plate_reader
    # TODO(final): the team has a Cytation1 and/or Cytation5 - confirm which, and which modules are fitted
    model: BioTek Cytation (1 or 5)
    modes: [absorbance, fluorescence, luminescence, imaging]
    absorbance_nm: [200, 999]      # OD600 for turbidity, OD530/590 for the MIC read, all within range
    plate_formats: [6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 384]
    reads_lidded: false            # the lid comes off to read

labware:
  # every count is TODO(final): the protocol shows what one run uses, not what is in the cupboard
  - load_name: corning_96_wellplate_360ul_flat
    kind: wellplate
    rows: 8
    cols: 12
    max_uL: 360                    # physical capacity
    working_uL: 200                # what the protocol actually fills; leaves headroom for mixing
    count: 10

  - load_name: opentrons_96_tiprack_300ul
    kind: tiprack
    tips: 96                       # 12 columns for an 8-channel pipette
    uL: 300
    count: 4

  - load_name: usascientific_12_reservoir_22ml
    kind: reservoir
    channels: 12
    max_mL: 22
    dead_mL: 2                     # tips aspirate 1 mm off the bottom and cannot reach the last few mL
    count: 2

capabilities:
  # Atmosphere belongs to a step, not to the lab (Emmy, 2026-11-08): the robot sets the plate up on the bench in
  # a few minutes, then a person carries it to an incubator overnight. Oxygen matters for the second of those.
  liquid_handling_atmosphere: [aerobic]     # the OT-2 is on the bench; no chamber, and none needed
  incubation_atmosphere: [aerobic, anaerobic]
  assumed:
    incubation_atmosphere: "anaerobic incubation (jars, sachets or an anaerobic incubator) assumed because the
      project is phenotyping anaerobic microbiome bacteria; confirm the lab has one before reporting a result"
  # How much air a species tolerates during the few minutes of setup. Aerotolerant anaerobes (B. fragilis) and
  # spore-formers are fine on the bench; the most oxygen-sensitive gut commensals (F. prausnitzii) are not, and
  # need either a chamber or pre-reduced media and speed. A panel entry may set `oxygen_tolerance` to say which.
  setup_air_exposure_minutes: 15            # TODO(final): time the real run
  incubation_C: [30, 37]
  shaking: unconfirmed             # TODO(final)
  solvent_limits:
    dmso_percent: 1.0              # the assay's ceiling, not the instrument's

reagents:
  # what is routinely on hand; a proposal naming something else needs a human
  - {id: camhb, name: "cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth", kind: medium}
  - {id: dmso, name: "DMSO", kind: solvent}
  - {id: water, name: "sterile water", kind: diluent}
  - {id: food_colouring, name: "food colouring", kind: dye}   # the dry-run stand-in for the demo

evidence_links.description: Must cover each experiment field: assay_type, atmosphere, concentration_unit, controls, dilution_factor, incubation_C, incubation_h, layout, medium, n_points, panel, readout, replicates, top_concentration, well_volume_uL

limits: Template is agent-curated; retain its TODOs and source applicability caveats.
Compilation uses separate sequential runs per compound-species pair with explicit sources.
Eight rows are physically filled per pair; requested replicate rows and surplus technical rows are recorded separately.
Only growth and sterility controls are implemented; do not silently remove requested extra controls.
This context is not feasibility approval or a simulation result.
